title: Polynomials
prerequisites: Definition of a polynomial and its degree.
Factorisation by splitting the middle term.
Ability to plot a graph from a table of values.
Knowledge of the remainder and factor theorems.

topics.title: Zeroes of a Polynomial and Their Graphical Meaning
topics.quick_summary: The zeroes of a polynomial are the x-coordinates of the points where its graph meets the x-axis, and a polynomial of degree n has at most n zeroes.
topics.real_life: The break-even points of a business, where profit is zero, are exactly the zeroes of the profit polynomial.

detailed.definition: A real number k is a zero of the polynomial p(x) if p(k) = 0. Geometrically, the zeroes are the x-coordinates of the points where the graph of y = p(x) intersects the x-axis.
detailed.key_idea: The graph tells you the number of real zeroes at a glance. A parabola cutting the axis twice has two zeroes, touching it once has one repeated zero, and missing it entirely has none.
detailed.working_principle: A linear polynomial has exactly one zero, a quadratic at most two and a cubic at most three. The graph of a quadratic is a parabola, opening upward if a > 0 and downward if a < 0.
applications: y = x² − 4 cuts the axis at x = 2 and x = −2.
y = x² + 1 never meets the x-axis, so it has no real zeroes.
y = (x − 3)² touches the axis at x = 3, a repeated zero.

points: A polynomial of degree n has AT MOST n real zeroes.
Zeroes are the x-coordinates of the graph's intersections with the x-axis.
A quadratic graph is a parabola: upward if a > 0, downward if a < 0.
Touching the x-axis means a repeated (equal) zero.
A cubic can have one, two or three real zeroes.
mistakes: Reading a y-intercept as a zero; zeroes lie on the x-axis.
Assuming every quadratic has two real zeroes.
Saying a degree-n polynomial has exactly n real zeroes; it has at most n.
topics.memory_hook: 'Zeroes are where the curve crosses the x-axis' — count the crossings, count the zeroes.
topics.advanced: The discriminant b² − 4ac decides the number of crossings before the graph is drawn: positive gives two, zero gives one, negative gives none. Algebra predicts the geometry exactly.

topics.title: Relationship Between Zeroes and Coefficients
topics.quick_summary: For a quadratic ax² + bx + c, the sum of the zeroes is −b/a and their product is c/a, which lets a polynomial be reconstructed from its zeroes.
topics.real_life: Knowing only the total and the product of two unknown quantities is enough to write down the quadratic they satisfy — a standard trick in word problems.

detailed.definition: If α and β are the zeroes of ax² + bx + c, then α + β = −b/a and αβ = c/a. For a cubic ax³ + bx² + cx + d with zeroes α, β, γ: α+β+γ = −b/a, αβ+βγ+γα = c/a, αβγ = −d/a.
detailed.key_idea: The signs alternate as the degree of the symmetric expression increases: −b/a, +c/a, −d/a. Remembering the alternating pattern is easier than memorising each result.
detailed.working_principle: A quadratic with given zeroes is written as k[x² − (sum)x + (product)], where k is any non-zero constant. Taking k = 1 gives the simplest such polynomial.
applications: Given one zero of a cubic, the other two are found by dividing and solving the quotient quadratic.
Symmetric expressions such as α² + β² are evaluated as (α+β)² − 2αβ.

mistakes: Writing the sum of the zeroes as +b/a instead of −b/a.
Forgetting to divide by a when the leading coefficient is not 1.
Omitting the arbitrary constant k when constructing a polynomial from its zeroes.
topics.memory_hook: 'Sum is minus b over a, Product is c over a' — and the signs alternate as you go up in degree.
topics.advanced: These are Vieta's formulas, valid for polynomials of any degree. They connect the coefficients to the elementary symmetric functions of the roots, a link that opens into Galois theory.

formulas.name: Zeroes and Coefficients of a Quadratic
formulas.variables: a, b, c = coefficients of ax² + bx + c; α, β = the two zeroes.
formulas.when_to_use: To find the sum or product of zeroes without solving, or to build a polynomial from its zeroes.
formulas.common_mistakes: Dropping the minus sign in the sum.
